items.text: Kafka introduced only for transaction-domain events, initially
RabbitMQ keeps existing notification workloads during the first migration phase; not replaced
Transaction IDs used as Kafka partition keys to preserve ordering
Consumers validate state transitions with a transaction state machine and reject invalid transitions
Temporary failures retried with exponential backoff and jitter
Invalid events eventually routed to a dead-letter topic for investigation
At-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers; exactly-once not required
Idempotency table with event ID, consumer name, processing status and timestamp checked before applying a state mutation
PostgreSQL remains the source of truth for idempotency records; Redis maybe later as an optimization
Benchmark read replicas before committing to the architecture
No production database schema changes deployed until the benchmark is completed
HTTP 400-level validation failures should not be retried; transient network failures and selected 5xx may be retried
Use idempotency keys for payment-provider requests
Reliability takes priority over aggressive retrying
Maximum retry window must be defined before implementation
OpenTelemetry tracing across the transaction lifecycle with a correlation ID through HTTP requests and Kafka messages

Metrics: transaction processing latency, Kafka consumer lag, event retry count, dead-letter queue volume, database connection pool utilization, PostgreSQL query latency, payment-provider latency, transaction failure rate
Alert thresholds defined per workload rather than globally
Kafka topics with transaction information must use encryption in transit
Consumer groups must have explicit access permissions
Services should authenticate with short-lived workload credentials rather than long-lived API keys
Sensitive payment information must never be in Kafka event payloads or application logs
Threat model covering event replay, unauthorized event publication, privilege escalation and cross-tenant data exposure
Encryption at rest should be enabled
Security review must be completed before production traffic moves to Kafka
Gradual rollout instead of a complete cutover, in phases: Kafka without behaviour change, then analytics, then inventory
Payment processing stays on the synchronous workflow until there is confidence in the event-driven architecture
Start with 1% of eligible traffic; raise to 10% if error rates and reconciliation stay acceptable for 48 hours
Further traffic increases require explicit approval from the engineering manager and SRE
No production migration begins until benchmark results, retry configuration, event-schema validation and security review readiness are reviewed
Promotional campaign in six weeks; migration timeline cannot be open-ended

Define retry policies, observability requirements and workload-specific alert thresholds
Complete the threat model covering replay attacks, unauthorized event publication and cross-tenant exposure
Create the phased migration schedule and approval criteria for increasing production traffic
Confirm the promotional campaign deadline and communicate business constraints to engineering
Intermittent latency spikes, duplicate transaction events and delayed downstream notifications

Inconsistent timeout and retry policies are contributing to cascading failures

Duplicate inventory reservations

Replication lag could break reconciliation reports that assume fresh data

The retry policy could increase transaction completion time
Current logging makes debugging distributed failures unnecessarily difficult
A fixed five-minute consumer lag threshold may not suit every topic
Exact retry intervals not finalized
Whether Redis should eventually be introduced as a deduplication cache
